core: The Reconstruction era, roughly 1865-1877, and the effort to rebuild the South and define freedom for about four million freedpeople
The Thirteenth Amendment (ratified December 6, 1865) abolishing slavery except as criminal punishment
The Fourteenth Amendment (ratified July 9, 1868): birthright citizenship, due process, equal protection
The Fifteenth Amendment (ratified February 3, 1870): no denial of the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude
The Freedmen's Bureau (Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands), created March 3, 1865: relief, schools, medical care, labor contracts, legal aid
Real but fragile gains: Black men voting and holding office (Hiram Revels 1870, Blanche K. Bruce), Black churches and schools
Presidential Reconstruction (Lincoln, Johnson) vs Radical/Congressional Reconstruction (Reconstruction Acts of 1867, military districts)
White backlash: Black Codes (1865-1866), the Ku Klux Klan (founded 1866), the White League and Red Shirts, racial terror
The Enforcement Acts / Ku Klux Klan Act (1870-1871) and their limited, fading enforcement
The disputed 1876 election (Hayes v. Tilden), the electoral commission, and the Compromise of 1877 withdrawing federal troops
The end of Reconstruction leading to Redeemer rule, disenfranchisement (literacy tests, poll taxes), segregation, and Jim Crow; Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
supporting: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 (passed over Johnson's veto)
The impeachment and acquittal of Andrew Johnson (1868)
The Panic of 1873 and waning Northern political will
The 'second founding' interpretation of the three amendments
outOfScope: The Civil War itself (referenced only as what preceded Reconstruction; handed to history:foundations:civil-war)
Slavery as an institution before the war (handed to history:foundations:slavery)
The detailed text and drafting of the Constitution (handed to history:foundations:constitution)
The Progressive Era and the twentieth-century civil-rights movement (later topics)

claims.claim: The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified December 6, 1865, abolished slavery and involuntary servitude in the United States except as punishment for a crime.
The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified July 9, 1868, established birthright citizenship and guaranteed all persons due process and equal protection of the laws, overturning the Dred Scott decision.
The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified February 3, 1870, barred denial of the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude, but did not prohibit literacy tests or poll taxes.

Congress created the Freedmen's Bureau (Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands) on March 3, 1865, within the War Department; it distributed rations, ran hospitals, helped establish schools, supervised labor contracts, and provided legal aid, with the bulk of its work done by December 1868 and formal closure in 1872.

Southern states passed Black Codes in 1865-1866 that forced freedpeople into restrictive labor contracts, punished leaving employers as vagrancy, and barred them from juries, firearms, and in some cases renting or owning land, in order to maintain slavery's social and economic order without the name.

Under the Reconstruction Acts of 1867, Congress divided ten former Confederate states into five military districts, required new state constitutions and ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment, and enfranchised Black men; hundreds of Black men held office, and Hiram Revels (1870) and Blanche K. Bruce became U.S. senators from Mississippi.

The Ku Klux Klan, founded in 1866 by former Confederates, and allied groups such as the White League and Red Shirts used violence and intimidation to suppress Black voting and political power; Congress briefly countered with the Enforcement Acts of 1870-1871, including the Ku Klux Klan Act.

In the disputed 1876 election, an electoral commission awarded the contested votes to Rutherford B. Hayes; the informal Compromise of 1877 secured Democratic acceptance in exchange for withdrawing the remaining federal troops from the South, ending Reconstruction.

After Reconstruction, Southern states used literacy tests, poll taxes, and violence to disenfranchise Black voters and built the Jim Crow system of legal segregation, which the Supreme Court upheld as 'separate but equal' in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896).

positions: Older 'Dunning School' / Lost-Cause view treating Reconstruction as a corrupt, vindictive 'tragic era' wrongly imposed on the South
Modern consensus (Foner and others) treating Reconstruction as a genuine, if unfinished, experiment in multiracial democracy defeated by organized white violence and political retreat
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the modern scholarly consensus, centers freedpeople, states the backlash factually, and explicitly rejects the Lost-Cause 'tragic era' framing, while distinguishing established facts (dates, events) from interpretation.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was generic boilerplate ('Reconstruction is a foundational concept in History...') with no substantive historical claims; it was discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced placeholder content with sourced history.

Avoided pinning a specific year to the Colfax Massacre in the lesson because a fetched OpenStax summary rendered it as 1872 while the established date is April 1873; the event is referenced only generally as White League/Klan-era terror to prevent asserting a contested date.
